# Project Overview

This project analyzes customer subscription behavior to identify meaningful customer segments and evaluate the effectiveness of promotional campaigns.

The analysis focuses on three business questions:

1. What types of customers generate the most value?
2. Which customer segments should be prioritized for retention or upselling?
3. Which customers continue using an upgraded subscription after receiving a promotion?

The project combines exploratory data analysis, factor analysis, customer segmentation using K-means clustering, demographic profiling, and pre/post campaign analysis.

# Data

The analysis uses four datasets:

- `SocioDemo`: customer demographic information
- `HoursMusic`: customer music preferences
- `HistoryData`: longitudinal subscription history
- `Action120`: promotional actions assigned to customers

```{r data}

load("StudentData.Rdata")

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(factoextra)
library(psy)
```

# 1. Preference Dimension Reduction

Customer music preferences contain several correlated dimensions. Factor analysis is used to summarize these preferences into broader behavioral dimensions.

```{r factor-analysis}
music_only <- HoursMusic[, c(
  "Mellow",
  "Unpretentous",
  "Sophisticated",
  "Intense",
  "Contemporary"
)]

factanal(music_only, factors = 2)
print(factanal(music_only, factors = 2), cutoff = .6)

cronbach(music_only[, c(1, 2, 5)])
cronbach(music_only[, c(3, 4)])
```

Based on the factor structure, two preference scales are constructed.

```{r preference-scales}
Refined_Passion <- apply(music_only[, 3:4], 1, mean)

Modern_Simplicity <- apply(
  music_only[, c(1, 2, 5)],
  1,
  mean
)
```

# 2. Subscription Behavior Over Time

Before segmenting customers, we examine how subscription choices evolve over time.

```{r subscription-behavior}
total_customers_by_time <- HistoryData %>%
  group_by(Time) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Customers = n_distinct(ID),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

subscription_behavior <- HistoryData %>%
  group_by(Time, Ad, Choice) %>%
  summarise(
    Count = n_distinct(ID),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(total_customers_by_time, by = "Time") %>%
  mutate(
    Proportion = Count / Total_Customers,
    Subscription_Tier = paste("Ad:", Ad, "Choice:", Choice)
  )

ggplot(
  subscription_behavior,
  aes(x = Time, y = Proportion, color = Subscription_Tier)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Subscription Behavior Over Time",
    x = "Time",
    y = "Proportion of Customers",
    color = "Subscription Tier"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The subscription mix changes over time, suggesting that customers differ in their willingness to pay for additional choice and an ad-free experience. These behavioral differences motivate a customer segmentation analysis.

# 3. Customer Value Segmentation

## Business Objective

The objective is to identify customer groups with different levels of **value** and **loyalty**.

Customer value is represented by average subscription profit, while loyalty is approximated by the length of observed subscription history.

```{r customer-profit}
plan_profit <- c(
  "Free" = 1.00,
  "No Ads" = 1.50,
  "Choice (with Ads)" = 3.00,
  "Choice (no Ads)" = 4.50
)

history_with_profit <- HistoryData %>%
  mutate(
    Profit = case_when(
      Ad == 1 & Choice == 1 ~ plan_profit["Free"],
      Ad == 1 & Choice == 2 ~ plan_profit["Choice (with Ads)"],
      Ad == 2 & Choice == 1 ~ plan_profit["No Ads"],
      Ad == 2 & Choice == 2 ~ plan_profit["Choice (no Ads)"],
      TRUE ~ plan_profit["Free"]
    )
  )

cluster_data <- history_with_profit %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Profit = sum(Profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total_Time = n(),
    Avg_Profit = mean(Profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## K-Means Segmentation

The variables are standardized before clustering so that differences in scale do not dominate the distance calculation.

```{r value-clustering}
cluster_data_norm <- cluster_data %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(Avg_Profit, Total_Time), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x)))
  )

set.seed(123)

kmeans_result <- kmeans(
  cluster_data_norm[, c("Avg_Profit", "Total_Time")],
  centers = 3,
  nstart = 20
)

cluster_data$Cluster <- factor(kmeans_result$cluster)

cluster_summary <- cluster_data %>%
  group_by(Cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    Average_Profit = mean(Avg_Profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    Average_Subscription_Time = mean(Total_Time, na.rm = TRUE),
    Customers = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

cluster_summary
```

```{r value-cluster-plot}
ggplot(
  cluster_data,
  aes(
    x = Avg_Profit,
    y = Total_Time,
    color = Cluster
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Customer Value and Loyalty Segments",
    x = "Average Profit",
    y = "Subscription Duration",
    color = "Cluster"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Customer Profiles

Clustering identifies behavioral groups, but business decisions require understanding who those customers are. The cluster assignments are therefore combined with demographic and preference information.

```{r customer-profiles}
preference_data <- HoursMusic %>%
  mutate(
    Refined_Passion = Refined_Passion,
    Modern_Simplicity = Modern_Simplicity
  )

cluster_with_demo <- cluster_data %>%
  left_join(preference_data, by = "ID") %>%
  left_join(SocioDemo, by = "ID")

cluster_demo_summary <- cluster_with_demo %>%
  group_by(Cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    Average_Profit = mean(Avg_Profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    Average_Subscription_Time = mean(Total_Time, na.rm = TRUE),
    Average_Age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE),
    Average_Income = mean(Salary, na.rm = TRUE),
    Female_Percentage = mean(Woman, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    Most_Common_City =
      names(sort(table(City), decreasing = TRUE))[1],
    Most_Common_Education =
      names(sort(table(Education), decreasing = TRUE))[1],
    Average_Refined_Passion =
      mean(Refined_Passion, na.rm = TRUE),
    Average_Modern_Simplicity =
      mean(Modern_Simplicity, na.rm = TRUE),
    Customers = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

cluster_demo_summary
```

## Business Interpretation

The resulting segments can support differentiated strategies.

- **High-value customers with shorter subscription histories** are important retention targets because losing them would reduce future customer value.
- **Long-term customers with moderate-to-high profitability** represent a loyal core that can be protected through loyalty benefits.
- **Lower-value customers** may represent an upselling opportunity when their engagement indicates potential interest in premium subscription features.

The objective is not simply to create clusters, but to translate behavioral differences into actionable customer strategies.

# 4. Promotion Effectiveness

## Business Objective

The second analysis examines customers who received a promotional action and asks whether they continued using the upgraded feature after the promotional period.

```{r promoted-customers}
promoted_customers <- Action120 %>%
  filter(Action %in% c(1, 2))

history_filtered <- HistoryData %>%
  filter(Time >= 120)

baseline_plan <- history_filtered %>%
  filter(Time == 120) %>%
  select(
    ID,
    Initial_Ad = Ad,
    Initial_Choice = Choice
  )

history_with_baseline <- history_filtered %>%
  left_join(baseline_plan, by = "ID")

merged_data <- promoted_customers %>%
  inner_join(history_with_baseline, by = "ID")
```

Only customers who were not already using the promoted feature are considered eligible.

```{r eligible-customers}
eligible_customers <- merged_data %>%
  filter(
    (Action == 1 & Initial_Ad == 1) |
    (Action == 2 & Initial_Choice == 1)
  )

eligible_customers %>%
  group_by(Action) %>%
  summarise(
    Eligible_Customers = n_distinct(ID),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

# 5. Post-Promotion Retention

For each customer, we calculate how long an upgraded subscription is sustained after the promotional period.

```{r upgrade-duration}
upgrade_duration <- history_with_baseline %>%
  filter(Time > 123) %>%
  arrange(ID, Time) %>%
  mutate(
    Sustained_Upgrade = ifelse(
      Ad > Initial_Ad | Choice > Initial_Choice,
      1,
      0
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Upgrade_Duration = sum(Sustained_Upgrade, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

eligible_customer_summary <- eligible_customers %>%
  distinct(ID, Action) %>%
  left_join(upgrade_duration, by = "ID") %>%
  mutate(
    Total_Upgrade_Duration =
      replace_na(Total_Upgrade_Duration, 0)
  )
```

```{r promotion-summary}
eligible_customer_summary %>%
  group_by(Action) %>%
  summarise(
    Customers = n(),
    Average_Upgrade_Duration =
      mean(Total_Upgrade_Duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

# 6. Promotion Response Segmentation

Customers receiving each promotional action can be grouped according to the duration for which they maintain the upgrade.

```{r promotion-clustering}
perform_promotion_clustering <- function(data, centers = 3) {

  scaled_duration <- scale(data$Total_Upgrade_Duration)

  set.seed(123)

  model <- kmeans(
    scaled_duration,
    centers = centers,
    nstart = 20
  )

  data %>%
    mutate(Cluster = factor(model$cluster))
}

promotion_clusters <- eligible_customer_summary %>%
  group_by(Action) %>%
  group_modify(
    ~ perform_promotion_clustering(.x, centers = 3)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

promotion_clusters %>%
  left_join(SocioDemo, by = "ID") %>%
  group_by(Action, Cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    Average_Upgrade_Duration =
      mean(Total_Upgrade_Duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    Average_Age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE),
    Average_Salary = mean(Salary, na.rm = TRUE),
    Customers = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

# 7. Pre/Post Campaign Profitability

Finally, the analysis compares customer profitability before and after the campaign.

```{r campaign-profitability}
action_impact <- history_with_profit %>%
  mutate(
    Time_Period = case_when(
      Time < 121 ~ "Pre-Campaign",
      Time > 123 ~ "Post-Campaign",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Time_Period)) %>%
  group_by(ID, Time_Period) %>%
  summarise(
    Profit = mean(Profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Time_Period,
    values_from = Profit
  )

campaign_results <- promotion_clusters %>%
  left_join(action_impact, by = "ID") %>%
  group_by(Action, Cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    Customers = n(),
    Average_Upgrade_Duration =
      mean(Total_Upgrade_Duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    Pre_Campaign_Profit =
      mean(`Pre-Campaign`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Post_Campaign_Profit =
      mean(`Post-Campaign`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

campaign_results
```

# 8. Business Recommendations

The analysis illustrates how customer analytics can support marketing and retention decisions.

**Retention:** High-value customers who maintain premium features but have relatively short histories should receive particular attention because retaining them can protect future customer value.

**Upselling:** Engaged customers in lower-profit subscription tiers can be targeted with relevant premium offers rather than applying promotions uniformly across the customer base.

**Campaign targeting:** Promotion response differs across customers. Segment-level response and post-campaign profitability can be used to identify populations for which promotions are most likely to create lasting value.

**Customer strategy:** Combining behavioral, demographic, preference, and profitability information produces more useful customer profiles than relying on a single characteristic.
